title: Athena's warning about Penelope
greek: οἶσθα γὰρ οἷος θυμὸς ἐνὶ στήθεσσι γυναικός (oistha gar hoios thumos eni stēthessi gunaikos)
short: To hurry Telemachus home, Athena tells him that Penelope's family is pressing her to marry Eurymachus and may take his property with her.
body: Athena appears to Telemachus in a dream-like vision at night in Sparta and works on his anxieties: Penelope's father and brothers urge her to marry Eurymachus, the most generous suitor; a remarried woman forgets the children of her first marriage; she may carry off treasure from the house. There is no sign elsewhere that Penelope is about to yield, and Athena's words are best read as a goad rather than a fact, though Penelope herself later says that her parents are urging her to marry (19.157-61). Ancient critics were uneasy: Monro reports that Aristophanes of Byzantium rejected 15.19 for its 'meanness' and that some critics rejected 15.24-6 because they lead nowhere; he answers that ancient critics judged Homeric sentiment by their own standards. The speech also warns Telemachus of the suitors' ambush and tells him to go first to the swineherd, joining the two strands of the plot.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 15.19 and 15.24-26.
Homer, Odyssey 19.157-161 (Penelope on her parents' pressure).
Homer, Odyssey 15.10-42.

title: The strait between Ithaca and Samos
greek: ἐν πορθμῷ Ἰθάκης τε Σάμοιό τε παιπαλοέσσης (en porthmōi Ithakēs te Samoio te paipaloessēs)
short: The channel between Ithaca and Same (Cephallenia), where the suitors wait in ambush for Telemachus.
body: Homer's Samos or Samē is the large island west of Ithaca later called Cephallenia (modern Kefalonia), not the Aegean Samos. The suitors' ship lies in wait at the islet of Asteris in this strait, as Book 4 described (4.842-7). Athena tells Telemachus to keep his ship 'far from the islands' and to sail by night as well as by day. Monro explains 'far from the islands' as keeping a wide berth from the islands associated with Ithaca (Dulichium, Same and Zacynthus), which lie 'towards Elis', and he rejects Strabo's theory that Telemachus made a long detour by the Echinades and landed on the far side of Ithaca. The geography of the return has been argued over since antiquity, and it bears on the modern debate about the location of Homeric Ithaca.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 15.33, 15.34 and 15.299-300.
Homer, Odyssey 4.842-847 (the ambush at Asteris).
Homer, Odyssey 15.28-35.

title: Menelaus' rule of hospitality
greek: χρὴ ξεῖνον παρεόντα φιλεῖν, ἐθέλοντα δὲ πέμπειν (chrē xeinon pareonta philein, ethelonta de pempein)
short: Menelaus states the golden mean of guest-friendship: neither keep a guest against his will nor hurry him away.
body: Menelaus says that excess in either direction is blameworthy: 'better is due measure in all things' (aisima, 15.71). It is equally wrong to send off an unwilling guest and to detain one eager to leave. Monro explains that too much kindness, shown by keeping a guest against his will, is as bad as sending him away too soon, but he regards the gnomic line 15.74 as a later addition, 'as such a line is apt to be'. The principle runs through the whole poem: Calypso detained Odysseus for seven years, the Phaeacians speed him home at once, and Telemachus will shortly avoid Nestor's overwhelming hospitality (15.195-201). Alexander Pope made the line proverbial in English: 'Welcome the coming, speed the parting guest' (Odyssey, Book 15, 1725), a line he reused in his Imitations of Horace, Satire II.ii.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 15.70 and 15.74.
Alexander Pope, The Odyssey of Homer (1725), Book XV; also Imitations of Horace, Satire II.ii.
Homer, Odyssey 15.68-74.

title: 'Through Hellas and mid-Argos'
greek: ἀν' Ἑλλάδα καὶ μέσον Ἄργος (an' Hellada kai meson Argos)
short: Menelaus offers to escort Telemachus on a tour of Greece collecting gifts; the meaning of the place-names was debated.
body: The phrase usually stands for the whole of Greece: Hellas originally a district of Thessaly in the north (Akhilleus' home in the Iliad), Argos the Peloponnese in the south. J. B. Bury (Journal of Hellenic Studies 15, 1895, 217-38) found it odd that Menelaus, who has just preached against detaining guests, should suddenly propose a long tour, and argued that Hellas here means the north coast of the Peloponnese, making the trip a short detour through Argolis and Achaea. Monro, summarising and rejecting Bury's case, holds that the phrase was a conventional epic commonplace (compare 1.344 = 4.726, 816) and that ancient manners may simply have required a host to make such an offer. Aristarchus athetised 15.78-85. Menelaus' promise that no host would send them away empty-handed shows the gift economy of the heroic aristocracy at work.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 15.80-85.
J. B. Bury, discussion of the names Hellas and Hellenes, Journal of Hellenic Studies 15 (1895) 217-38, as summarised by Monro.
Homer, Odyssey 1.344 (the same phrase).

title: Helen's robe for Telemachus' bride
greek: μνῆμ' Ἑλένης χειρῶν, πολυηράτου ἐς γάμου ὥρην (mnēm' Helenēs cheirōn, poluēratou es gamou hōrēn)
short: Helen gives Telemachus a robe she wove herself, to be worn by his future bride; the description echoes Hecuba's robe in the Iliad.
body: Menelaus gives a cup and the silver mixing-bowl promised in Book 4; Helen chooses from her chests the robe 'fairest in its broideries and the amplest', which 'shone like a star, and lay beneath all the rest'. These lines (15.107-8) repeat Il. 6.294-5, where Hecuba chooses the finest robe to offer to Athena in a vain prayer for Troy. Helen herself is a weaver in the Iliad, working the battles of Greeks and Trojans into a purple web (Il. 3.125-8). The gift is called a mnēma, a memorial or keepsake: Telemachus' bride will wear the work of the woman for whom the war was fought. Until then it is to lie with Penelope, a delicate pairing of the faithless and the faithful wife. Monro notes that the infinitive keisthai, 'let it lie', has a gentler tone than an imperative.

sources.cite: Homer, Iliad 6.289-295 (Hecuba's robe).
Homer, Iliad 3.125-128 (Helen weaving).
D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 15.128.

title: The eagle and the goose: Helen's prophecy
greek: αἰετὸς ἀργὴν χῆνα φέρων ὀνύχεσσι πέλωρον, ἥμερον ἐξ αὐλῆς (aietos argēn chēna pherōn onuchessi pelōron, hēmeron ex aulēs)
short: An eagle seizes a tame goose on the right; Helen reads it as Odysseus returning from the wild to destroy the suitors who fatten in his house.
body: The line describing the eagle adapts an Iliadic omen in which an eagle carries a monstrous serpent (Il. 12.201-2); Monro notes that the adjective pelōron, 'monstrous', fits a serpent but gives a mock-heroic touch when applied to a goose. Birds appearing on the right were lucky, and Monro explains that the eagle crosses the path of the chariot 'from left to right' in front of the horses; he also notes the narrative pattern of a brief statement followed by detailed description. Peisistratus asks whether the sign is for Menelaus or for them, and while Menelaus ponders how to interpret it (hupokrinaito, 'expound'), Helen speaks first: the eagle from the mountains is Odysseus, the domestic goose the suitors fattened in the palace. The interpretation looks ahead to Penelope's dream in Book 19, in which an eagle kills her twenty pet geese and declares itself her husband (19.535-53). Helen's readiness to prophesy matches her authority in Book 4, where she drugged the wine and told the first story about Odysseus (4.219-64). Telemachus' grateful reply, 'I will pray to thee as to a god', anticipates Helen's later cult in Sparta.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 15.160 and 15.170, and Appendix II, p. 330.
Homer, Odyssey 19.535-553 (Penelope's dream of the eagle and geese).
Homer, Odyssey 4.219-264 (Helen's drug and story).

anchor: Lead me not past my ship
title: Telemachus avoids Nestor's hospitality
greek: μή με παρὲξ ἄγε νῆα (mē me parex age nēa)
short: Telemachus asks Peisistratus to drop him at his ship so that Nestor cannot delay him with excessive kindness.
body: Menelaus' maxim about not detaining guests is put immediately into practice. Telemachus appeals to his friendship with Peisistratus, 'friends from of old by reason of our fathers' friendship', the inherited guest-friendship that bound aristocratic families across generations. Peisistratus weighs his obligations and chooses the friend over the father: he unloads the gifts at the ship and warns Telemachus to leave before Nestor, 'so masterful is his spirit', comes down to fetch him. Monro notes that this shows, as Strabo observed, that the city of Pylos lay some distance from the shore, and that the word huperbios, 'overbearing', used of Nestor here and borrowed from the Iliad, is only half-serious. The episode gives a humorous touch to the respected old king of Book 3 and closes the Telemachy.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 15.199 and 15.212.
Homer, Odyssey 15.193-221.
Homer, Odyssey 3.346-355 (Nestor's insistence on hospitality).

title: Melampus, ancestor of Theoclymenus
greek: Μελάμποδος ἔκγονος (Melampodos ekgonos)
short: The famous seer from whom the prophet Theoclymenus descends; his story of cattle-raiding and imprisonment is told in brief.
body: Melampus ('Black-foot') was the archetypal seer of Greek legend. The Odyssey alludes to his story twice, unnamed in the Underworld catalogue (11.287-97) and by name here. Neleus of Pylos would give his daughter Pero only to the man who brought him the cattle of Iphiclus from Phylace; Melampus undertook the raid for his brother Bias, was imprisoned for a year in the house of Phylacus, won release by prophecy, drove the cattle to Pylos, punished Neleus, who had seized his property, and gave Pero to his brother. He then settled in Argos and became a ruler there. Fuller versions are in Apollodorus (Library 1.9.11-12), and Herodotus says Melampus won part of the kingdom of Argos by curing its women of madness (9.34). Monro explains that Theoclymenus is Melampus' great-grandson. The long digression gives the stranger a prophetic pedigree, preparing us to trust his later visions (17.151-61; 20.350-7).

sources.cite: Homer, Odyssey 11.287-297 (the unnamed seer and Pero).
Apollodorus, Library 1.9.11-12.
Herodotus, Histories 9.34.
D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 15.225-226.

title: The Erinys 'dasplētis'
greek: θεὰ δασπλῆτις Ἐρινύς (thea dasplētis Erinus)
short: The avenging spirit who sent Melampus 'blindness of heart'; her rare epithet dasplētis may mean 'frightful' or 'smiter of houses'.
body: The Erinyes (Furies) avenge wrongs, especially within families and against oaths. Here an Erinys has put atē, 'terrible blindness of heart', into Melampus' mind, the folly that led him into his dangerous enterprise. The epithet dasplētis is found only here in Homer. LSJ translates it 'horrid, frightful', noting its later use of Hecate (Theocritus 2.14). Monro instead explains it as 'smiter of houses', comparing teichesiplētēs, 'stormer of walls', and connecting the first element with the des- of despotēs, 'house-master'; Murray's 'who brings houses to ruin' follows Monro. The disagreement is a good example of how uncertain the meaning of rare Homeric words can be, and of how a translator's choice of commentary shapes the English a student reads.

sources.cite: Liddell-Scott-Jones, A Greek-English Lexicon, s.v. δασπλῆτις.
D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 15.234.
Homer, Odyssey 15.233-234.

title: Amphiaraus and Eriphyle's necklace
greek: ἀλλ' ὄλετ' ἐν Θήβῃσι γυναίων εἵνεκα δώρων (all' olet' en Thēbēisi gunaiōn heineka dōrōn)
short: The seer Amphiaraus, loved by Zeus and Apollo, died at Thebes because his wife Eriphyle was bribed to send him to war.
body: Amphiaraus, great-grandson of Melampus, foresaw that the expedition of the Seven against Thebes would fail and that he would die in it, but his wife Eriphyle, bribed with the necklace of Harmonia by Polyneices, made him go. He vanished into the earth at Thebes. The Odyssey has already named Eriphyle among the women in the Underworld, 'who took precious gold for her own husband's life' (11.326-7); Apollodorus (Library 3.6.2) tells the full story, and Pausanias describes the scene on the Chest of Cypselus at Olympia (5.17.7-8). 'Woman's gifts' (gunaia dōra) means gifts given to a woman. Monro explains 'the threshold of old age' (15.246) as meaning that he never fairly set foot in old age, and records that Plutarch (Consolation to Apollonius 17) found here the idea that those whom the gods love die young, a reading Monro thinks the poet did not intend.

sources.cite: Homer, Odyssey 11.326-327 (Eriphyle).
Apollodorus, Library 3.6.2.
Pausanias, Description of Greece 5.17.7-8 (Chest of Cypselus).
D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 15.246.

title: Cleitus, carried off by Dawn
greek: ἀλλ' ἦ τοι Κλεῖτον χρυσόθρονος ἥρπασεν Ἠὼς κάλλεος εἵνεκα οἷο (Kleiton chrusothronos hērpasen Ēōs kalleos heineka hoio)
short: One of Theoclymenus' ancestors was taken by the goddess Dawn for his beauty to live among the immortals.
body: Dawn (Eos) was famous for carrying off beautiful young men. Calypso complains of the gods' jealousy when Dawn took Orion, whom Artemis then killed (5.121-4); Dawn's husband Tithonus rises from her bed at the opening of Book 5; Hesiod lists her children by Tithonus and by Cephalus (Theogony 984-91). Cleitus is otherwise unknown. His abduction is a pleasant fate, since he lives with the immortals, and it contrasts with the death of his cousin Amphiaraus a few lines earlier: in this genealogy one branch is taken up to the gods, the other swallowed by the earth. The other son, Polypheides, became the greatest seer after Amphiaraus' death and settled at Hyperesia (in Achaea) after quarrelling with his father; Theoclymenus is his son.

sources.cite: Homer, Odyssey 5.121-124 (Dawn and Orion).
Hesiod, Theogony 984-991 (Dawn's lovers).
D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 15.256.

title: Theoclymenus, the fugitive seer
greek: Θεοκλύμενος δ' ὄνομ' ἦεν (Theoklumenos d' onom' ēen)
short: A prophet who has killed a kinsman and asks Telemachus for passage; his supplication is Telemachus' first act as a host.
body: Theoclymenus (the name suggests 'famed by' or 'hearing the god') approaches while Telemachus is sacrificing at the ship and supplicates him 'by thine offerings and by the god'. Like the false Cretan of 13.256-86, he is a killer fleeing the vengeance of his victim's kin, a common reason for exile in Homeric society; such men depended on the protection of strangers. Telemachus accepts him on board without hesitation and later entrusts him to Peiraeus (15.539-46). Monro discusses the formula 'my father is Odysseus, if ever he was' (15.267-8), arguing that it is an emphatic assurance ('as surely as there was a Ulysses'), not an expression of doubt. Theoclymenus has a small but striking role: he interprets the hawk omen (15.531-4), assures Penelope that Odysseus is already in Ithaca (17.151-61), and in Book 20 has an eerie vision of the suitors' doom (20.350-7).

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 15.225 and 15.268.
Homer, Odyssey 20.350-357 (Theoclymenus' vision).
Homer, Odyssey 17.151-161 (his prophecy to Penelope).

title: Telemachus' voyage home
greek: βὰν δὲ παρὰ Κρουνοὺς καὶ Χαλκίδα καλλιρέεθρον ... ἡ δὲ Φεὰς ἐπέβαλλεν ... νήσοισιν ἐπιπροέηκε θοῇσιν
short: The ship coasts north past Crouni, Chalcis, Pheae and Elis, then heads for the 'sharp' (or 'swift') islands.
body: These lines raise textual and geographical problems discussed at length by Monro. Line 295 ('they passed Crouni and Chalcis') is absent from nearly all manuscripts of the Odyssey (Monro's Additional Notes record one that has it) and is known chiefly from Strabo's quotation (Geography 8.3.26) and from a version in the Homeric Hymn to Apollo (425-9), where the order of lines differs; Monro accepts it as genuine and places it before 298. He reads Pheae (Pheia, a town near the headland of Katakolo south of Elis) rather than the manuscripts' Pherae, since there is no Pherae on this coast. The phrase nēsoisin thoēisin is obscure: Strabo took the 'sharp' islands to be some of the Echinades, but Monro thinks the word unexplained and suspects that 'the islands' are simply Dulichium, Same and Zacynthus. The voyage ends with Telemachus 'pondering whether he should escape death or be taken'.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 15.295-298 and 15.299-300, with Additional Notes on 15.295.
Homeric Hymn 3, To Apollo 425-429.
Strabo, Geography 8.3.26 (Casaubon p. 350), as quoted and discussed by Monro.

anchor: Hermes, the messenger, who lends grace
title: Hermes, patron of service
greek: Ἑρμείαο ἕκητι διακτόρου, ὅς ῥά τε πάντων ἀνθρώπων ἔργοισι χάριν καὶ κῦδος ὀπάζει (Hermeiao hekēti diaktorou)
short: Testing Eumaeus, the beggar boasts that thanks to Hermes no one can rival him at serving: building fires, splitting wood, carving and pouring wine.
body: Odysseus proposes to go to town and offer his services to the suitors, claiming that Hermes gives him unrivalled skill at drēstosunē, the work of a servant. Hermes is a natural patron: in the Homeric Hymn to Hermes the infant god invents fire-making with fire-sticks, slaughters and roasts cattle and divides the meat (lines 108-37), exactly the tasks the beggar lists. He is also the god of luck and of herdsmen, honoured with a portion at Eumaeus' sacrifice (14.435). Monro explains that the infinitives (piling a fire, splitting logs, carving, roasting, pouring) define the kind of service meant. The boast is ironic: the king of Ithaca advertises himself as a waiter. Eumaeus' horrified reply shows that he has passed the test, since he wants to keep his guest safe from the suitors' outrage.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 15.317 and 15.322.
Homeric Hymn 4, To Hermes 108-137.
Homer, Odyssey 15.319-324.

title: The 'iron heaven'
greek: τῶν ὕβρις τε βίη τε σιδήρεον οὐρανὸν ἵκει (tōn hubris te biē te sidēreon ouranon hikei)
short: Eumaeus says the suitors' outrage and violence reach the sky, pictured as a vault of metal.
body: Homer imagines the sky as a solid metal dome: elsewhere it is 'bronze' (chalkeos) or 'of much bronze', and here 'iron'. LSJ cites this line under sidēreos for 'the iron sky, the firmament, which the ancients held to be of metal'. The Iliad has a close parallel in which the 'iron din' of battle reaches the 'bronze heaven' (Il. 17.424-5). The image of wrongdoing that rises to heaven gives Eumaeus' warning a moral force, since what reaches the sky reaches the gods who live there. The key word hubris, arrogant violence that disregards the rights of others, is constantly applied to the suitors and is the charge on which they will be punished. The same line is spoken again by Odysseus himself, still disguised as a beggar, when he talks to Eumaeus at 17.565.

sources.cite: Liddell-Scott-Jones, A Greek-English Lexicon, s.v. σιδήρεος.
Homer, Iliad 17.424-425 (iron din and bronze heaven).
Homer, Odyssey 17.565 (the line repeated).

title: The 'cursed belly'
greek: ἀλλ' ἕνεκ' οὐλομένης γαστρός κακὰ κήδε' ἔχουσιν (all' henek' oulomenēs gastros kaka kēde' echousin)
short: The beggar names hunger, the 'accursed belly', as the force that drives wanderers to endure every hardship.
body: The belly (gastēr) is a recurring theme of the Odyssey's beggar books. Odysseus already called it shameless and insistent among the Phaeacians (7.216-21); in Ithaca he says it drives men to fit out ships against enemies (17.286-9), and he blames it when he agrees to box with Irus (18.53-4). Monro, following W. Schulze, explains oulomenos not as 'destructive' but as 'miserable, accursed', an intransitive form of the verb 'to perish' (olomenos), and finds a slightly mock-heroic effect in applying such a word to the stomach; LSJ cites this line under the same sense. Hunger is the defining condition of the beggar, the role Odysseus has adopted, and the emphasis on it underlines how far the hero has descended from the king who once fed others.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 15.344.
Liddell-Scott-Jones, A Greek-English Lexicon, s.v. οὐλόμενος.
Homer, Odyssey 17.286-289 (the belly drives men to sea).

anchor: on the threshold of old age
title: 'On the threshold of old age'
greek: ἐπὶ γήραος οὐδῷ (epi gēraos oudōi)
short: A formula for old age itself, used of Laertes, whom Odysseus left 'on the threshold of old age'.
body: The 'threshold' (oudos) here does not mean the entrance to old age, but its last stage, the doorway out of life; Priam uses the phrase of himself when he begs Hector to come inside the walls (Il. 22.60), and Akhilleus of his own aged father Peleus (Il. 24.487). Monro, discussing 15.246, says the point there is that Amphiaraus 'never fairly set foot in old age'. In Plato's Republic Socrates asks old Cephalus what it is like to be 'on the threshold of old age', quoting the poets (Republic 1, 328e). Odysseus' question about his parents leads Eumaeus to tell of Laertes' grief and of the death of Odysseus' mother from sorrow, already reported by her ghost (11.197-203).

sources.cite: Homer, Iliad 22.60 (Priam).
Homer, Iliad 24.487 (Peleus).
Plato, Republic 1, 328e.
D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 15.246.

title: Ctimene, Odysseus' sister
greek: ἅμα Κτιμένῃ τανυπέπλῳ (hama Ktimenēi tanupeplōi)
short: Odysseus' youngest sister, named only here; Eumaeus was raised alongside her before she was married off to Same.
body: Ctimene is mentioned nowhere else in Homer. Anticleia brought up the young slave Eumaeus with her own youngest daughter, and honoured him 'little less than her own children'. When the two came of age, Ctimene was married to a man of Same (Cephallenia) and her family received 'countless bridal gifts' (the bride-price paid by the groom), while Eumaeus was given clothes and sandals and sent to the fields. Monro discusses the 'pregnant' use of 'they gave her to Same', meaning 'gave her in marriage and sent her there'. The episode explains Eumaeus' near-filial bond with the family and his grief for Anticleia, and it shows how marriage moved daughters between households and islands, the background to the suitors' claims on Penelope.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 15.367 and 15.373.
Homer, Odyssey 15.361-370.
Liddell-Scott-Jones, A Greek-English Lexicon, s.v. ἕδνον.

title: The pleasure of remembered sorrow
greek: μετὰ γάρ τε καὶ ἄλγεσι τέρπεται ἀνήρ, ὅς τις δὴ μάλα πολλὰ πάθῃ καὶ πόλλ' ἐπαληθῇ (meta gar te kai algesi terpetai anēr)
short: Eumaeus invites his guest to share the 'joy' of recalling past sufferings, a famous Homeric reflection on storytelling.
body: The long winter nights leave time for sleep and for tales, and Eumaeus proposes that they take delight 'each in the other's grievous woes'. The thought that suffering becomes pleasurable once it is past and told is central to the Odyssey, a poem full of tales of hardship told at feasts. Aristotle quotes these lines in the Rhetoric (1.11, 1370b) when explaining why memory can give pleasure even of painful things, together with a tragic line on the sweetness of remembering toils once one is safe. Virgil gives the idea its most famous form when Aeneas encourages his shipwrecked men: 'perhaps one day it will be a pleasure to remember even these things' (Aeneid 1.203). The swineherd's tale that follows is itself a story of kidnapping and slavery turned into after-dinner narrative.

sources.cite: Aristotle, Rhetoric 1.11, 1370b (quoting Od. 15.400-401).
Virgil, Aeneid 1.203.
Homer, Odyssey 15.398-401.

anchor: There is an isle called Syria
title: Syria above Ortygia: Eumaeus' homeland
greek: νῆσός τις Συρίη κικλήσκεται ... Ὀρτυγίης καθύπερθεν, ὅθι τροπαὶ ἠελίοιο (Suriē ... Ortugiēs kathuperthen, hothi tropai ēelioio)
short: A blessed island without famine or disease, ruled by Eumaeus' royal father Ctesius; its location was disputed in antiquity.
body: Eumaeus reveals that he was born a prince: his father Ctesius son of Ormenus ruled both cities of Syria, 'a man like to the immortals'. The island is nearly paradisal: rich in herds, wine and wheat, free from famine and hateful sickness, its people dying in old age by the 'gentle shafts' of Apollo and Artemis. Readers have identified Syria with the Cycladic island Syros and Ortygia ('Quail Island') with nearby Delos, but Monro regards both as mythical places, the 'turning-points of the sun' giving them a cosmic character, like Circe's island with its 'risings of the sun' (12.3-4). LSJ notes that tropai ēelioio here probably denotes a point on the horizon, perhaps where the sun sets, though later the phrase meant the solstices. Artemis killed Orion 'in Ortygia' (5.123), another hint that the name belonged to legend.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 15.403.
Liddell-Scott-Jones, A Greek-English Lexicon, s.v. τροπή.
Homer, Odyssey 5.121-124 (Orion killed in Ortygia).

title: Phoenician traders
greek: Φοίνικες ναυσίκλυτοι ἤλυθον ἄνδρες, τρῶκται, μυρί' ἄγοντες ἀθύρματα (Phoinikes nausiklutoi ... trōktai)
short: The seafaring merchants of Sidon and Tyre, in the Odyssey shrewd traders in trinkets who also kidnap and sell people.
body: Phoenicians appear in all three of the stories told to or by Eumaeus. In the first Cretan lie they kindly carry the narrator (13.271-86); in the second a Phoenician 'well versed in guile' plans to sell him in Libya (14.288-97); here they seduce a slave-woman and carry off the child Eumaeus, selling him to Laertes. They are called trōktai, which LSJ glosses 'greedy knaves' (literally 'gnawers'); Monro observes that nouns of this form often have a hostile or contemptuous sense, perhaps suggesting thieving vermin. They stay a whole year trading, bringing 'countless trinkets' (athurmata). Herodotus begins his Histories with a similar story: Phoenician merchants trading at Argos for days who seize the king's daughter Io (1.1). The poem reflects the real role of Phoenician merchants in the Mediterranean of the eighth and seventh centuries BC, seen through Greek suspicion of foreign traders.

sources.cite: Liddell-Scott-Jones, A Greek-English Lexicon, s.v. τρώκτης.

title: The amber necklace
greek: χρύσεον ὅρμον ἔχων, μετὰ δ' ἠλέκτροισιν ἔερτο (chruseon hormon echōn, meta d' ēlektroisin eerto)
short: A Phoenician trader shows a gold necklace strung with amber in the palace as the signal for the nurse to escape with the child.
body: The Phoenician nurse, herself a kidnapped daughter of Arybas of Sidon (Monro suspects a Phoenician name, perhaps related to Hasdrubal), has sworn the traders to take her home and offers the king's small son as her 'passage money' (epibathron, LSJ). The signal is a necklace (hormos) of gold strung with pieces of ēlektron; LSJ and Monro agree that here the plural means pieces of amber, not the gold-silver alloy also called electrum. While the queen and her maids handle the necklace and bargain over it, the trader nods to the nurse, who leads the child away, stealing three goblets on the way. A similar gift, a necklace of gold strung with amber 'like the sun', is given to Penelope by Eurymachus (18.295-6). The scene is a vivid picture of trade, desire and betrayal in an aristocratic household.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 15.426 and 15.460.

title: The nurse's death at sea
greek: ἄντλῳ δ' ἐνδούπησε πεσοῦσ' ὡς εἰναλίη κήξ (antlōi d' endoupēse pesous' hōs einaliē kēx)
short: On the seventh day Artemis strikes the treacherous nurse dead; she falls into the hold like a diving sea-bird and is thrown overboard.
body: Sudden death of women is attributed to Artemis in Homer, as sudden death of men is to Apollo (compare 11.172-3, 11.324). The nurse falls into the bilge 'like a sea-bird', kēx, which LSJ thinks may be the tern; the sound-word endoupēse is, as Monro suggests, an adaptation, almost a parody, of the Iliad's formula for a warrior's fall, 'he fell with a thud'. The sailors throw her body to the seals and fish. The episode gives the treacherous slave a kind of poetic justice while leaving the child Eumaeus alone among strangers, 'my heart sore stricken'. The ship is then carried to Ithaca, where Laertes buys the boy, which brings the tale home to the hut where it is being told.

sources.cite: Liddell-Scott-Jones, A Greek-English Lexicon, s.v. κήξ.

anchor: side by side with the evil
title: Good mixed with evil from Zeus
greek: σοὶ μὲν παρὰ καὶ κακῷ ἐσθλὸν ἔθηκε Ζεύς (soi men para kai kakōi esthlon ethēke Zeus)
short: Odysseus consoles Eumaeus that Zeus has mixed good with his evil, since he found a kind master; Odysseus himself still wanders.
body: The thought recalls Akhilleus' famous image in Iliad 24 of the two jars on Zeus' threshold, one of evils and one of blessings: to some men Zeus gives a mixture, to others only evils (Il. 24.527-33). Odysseus places Eumaeus among the fortunate: kidnapped and enslaved, he nevertheless came to a master who feeds him 'with kindness', so that he lives well. Monro notes that kakōi is placed between kai and esthlon to bring the contrasted 'evil' and 'good' side by side. The comparison is also self-pity in disguise: the speaker presents himself as a wanderer still without home, a description true of Odysseus for twenty years but about to cease. The exchange of life stories creates a bond between master and slave before either knows the other's identity.

sources.cite: Homer, Iliad 24.527-533 (the jars of Zeus).

title: The hawk and the dove: Theoclymenus' omen
greek: κίρκος, Ἀπόλλωνος ταχὺς ἄγγελος (kirkos, Apollōnos tachus angelos)
short: A hawk plucking a dove flies on the right; Theoclymenus declares that Odysseus' house will remain the most kingly in Ithaca.
body: Telemachus has just suggested that Theoclymenus lodge with Eurymachus, 'whom the men of Ithaca look upon as on a god' and who seems likely to marry Penelope. At once a hawk flies past on the right, tearing a dove and scattering its feathers between the ship and Telemachus. The hawk is called Apollo's 'swift messenger', as the eagle is Zeus' 'swift messenger' in the Iliad (24.292-3). Theoclymenus takes Telemachus aside and declares that no house in Ithaca is more kingly than his. Monro explains the narrative logic: the mention of Eurymachus exists to provoke the prophecy, after which the plan to send the stranger to him is quietly dropped and Telemachus promises hospitality through his friend Peiraeus. The omen pairs with the eagle and goose in Sparta (15.160-78): both show a bird of prey destroying a weaker bird, the suitors' fate.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 15.519 and 15.532.
